paragraphs.text: This is another very strange board, with the 5 wheat isolated out in no-man’s-land. I kind of like the 9-5-10 because it gives us wood and brick. What also interests me is the possible 8-10 to 8-5 idea, although somebody will probably take that. Alternatively, the 8-10-4 gives us access to sheep, and the 6-9-3 could also run toward an 8-10 spot.
uncertainties: The exact meaning of the proposed route from 8-10 to 8-5 is unclear, and 8-10 refers to multiple possible intersections.

paragraphs.text: The 8-4-10 also has an interesting idea. In the worst case, we can play off some wood and work that angle; in the best case, we could go toward an 8-10 below or a 5-10 above. There is also a 3:1 port and a brick port in the area, and the sheep is at least somewhat useful. It feels pretty good, even though the whole position is still kind of bad.
uncertainties: The captions do not uniquely establish which route or position the nearby ports belong to; the directional 8-10 and 5-10 references remain ambiguous.

paragraphs.text: I am concerned about the 6-3-11, though I cannot quite finish that thought. Still, I want to trust my gut and just do it. The 6-4-11 is another option and is not bad—you can take the ore—but this is a tricky spot, and I am not convinced by that line either.
uncertainties: The concern about 6-3-11 and the objection after taking ore are both cut off in the captions.

paragraphs.text: I didn’t really see what 8-4-3 would lead to next. By contrast, going 8-4-10 opened up the brick port and the 3:1, while also giving me sheep. I thought we might then play off something like 6-5-11 and simply focus on production; if things went especially well, we could potentially take 5-10 up toward 8-10. I liked that plan.
uncertainties: The intended 5-10 and 8-10 intersections are not uniquely identifiable from the number references alone.

paragraphs.text: I considered 8-5-10 to have the same pips as 9-5-10, but preferred having sheep and knowing I could pick up wood on the way back; the lack of sheep made 9-5-10 less appealing. Still, I didn’t think our position was great. Whoever could connect 5-10 to 8-10 would be in a strong spot, and 6-9-3 could support that. The more I looked at it, the more I wondered whether the angle had been to take 6-9-3, go left, potentially build at 5-2, and keep that 3 to ourselves. That was certainly an option, though I still liked the port play because it offered both the 3:1 and brick port.

It is unclear whether “that 3” means the 3-numbered tile or a 3:1 port.

uncertainties: The exact 5-10 and downward 8-10 locations remain ambiguous.

paragraphs.text: We actually have full access to both the brick port and the 3:1 port.

It’s kind of crazy that the fourth player has been given the best ore, but it isn’t obvious what to do about that. There is an angle involving the 6-4-3 spot, but the wheat is the problem—the wheat here is awful, which makes the decision really tough.

I'm hoping Black pairs this brick with the best wood, perhaps going for the 4-6 spots or a 6-4-11 angle. I think the fourth player will take an 8-4-3 because it seems like their better option, although it is unclear what to do with it afterward. Maybe they could play two settlements side by side, but they would need wood and a good port; the sheep port is poor, while the ore port is at least okay.

paragraphs.text: Another option is to pair an 8-4-3 with the 6-4-11 and take over much of the left side of the board. The idea would be to make a couple of trades and reach a 3:1 port, perhaps using surplus sheep in ore trades. The ore port adds a little value, but not much.

Now that another player appears to have access to the sheep port, I think we are set up nicely for a four to remain available, and I really want him to point his road upward.

paragraphs.text: I need to make some big headway before that becomes a really big issue. I considered taking the 5-5-10 and running to the 8, but I’m going with the 8-4 and then planning to city the 8-4-10. With that plan, I can improve my ore, wheat, and sheep production.

paragraphs.text: We got very lucky.
A lot of things went our way.
A lot of things went our way. We got very timely dice, and the rolls felt maxed out, even though we actually rolled the fewest cards. The real difference was the efficiency of our development cards.

Doing that while playing coastal port and drawing no victory points was not easy. I first thought we might have had a Monopoly, then corrected myself: we pulled a Year of Plenty, a Road Building card, and, I think, only knights.
